title: Effects of a Sequential Pelvic Floor Muscle Training Program on Urinary Continence Recovery After Transurethral Prostate Enucleation: A Randomized Controlled Trial
content: Background/Objectives: Early urinary incontinence after transurethral prostate enucleation impairs recovery and quality of life. We evaluated a nurse-led sequential pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) program in this setting. Methods: Sixty men undergoing prostate enucleation for benign prostatic hyperplasia were allocated 1:1 to sequential PFMT or routine care in a single-center, open-label randomized trial with 3-month follow-up. Continence was classified at a point assessment as no pad use and no self-reported involuntary leakage at each visit. The registered primary outcome, time to recovery of continence, could not be analysed because no time-to-event data were available; the primary endpoints reported here were therefore the proportions continent immediately after catheter removal and at 1 week. Secondary outcomes covered perioperative recovery, urodynamics, urinary symptoms, pad-test leakage, and quality of life. The trial was prospectively registered (Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR2400085870). Results: Immediate continence occurred in 28/30 (93.3%) versus 17/30 (56.7%) participants (risk difference 36.7 percentage points; risk ratio 1.65, 95% CI 1.19–2.28; P = 0.002); at 1 week, 29/30 (96.7%) versus 22/30 (73.3%) (23.3 points; risk ratio 1.32, 95% CI 1.05–1.65; P = 0.026). Time to first ambulation (−9.50 hours, 95% CI −12.47 to −6.53), postoperative stay (−1.43 days, 95% CI −2.01 to −0.85), and 3-month ICIQ-SF score (−2.20, 95% CI −2.80 to −1.60) all favoured sequential PFMT. No serious adverse events were observed. Conclusions: Sequential PFMT was associated with higher early continence rates and faster perioperative recovery. Given the open-label, single-center, small sample, exploratory secondary analyses, and the registered primary outcome that could not be analysed as specified, these findings are hypothesis-generating and warrant confirmation in a larger trial with concealed allocation and a prespecified analysis plan.
